analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue and prosecute police for misconduct and creates a national misconduct registry.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced September 15, 2025 with 136 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to three House committees; none has taken it up and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make police officers easier to hold accountable in court: it lowers the intent standard for convicting an officer of a federal civil-rights violation, limits qualified immunity (the court-made doctrine that often shields officers from lawsuits), and lets the Justice Department subpoena records in pattern-of-misconduct investigations. It bans no-knock warrants in drug cases, restricts chokeholds and carotid holds, sets a tighter national standard for when deadly force is allowed, and requires federal officers to wear body cameras. It also creates a searchable national registry of police misconduct records, requires detailed reporting on stops, searches, and use of force by race, and directs new training on racial bias and the duty to intervene. States that do not comply can lose federal police grant money.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are stopped, searched, or subject to police force — disproportionately Black and brown Americans — gain new tools to sue officers, a public registry to check an officer's record before encounters or hires, and federal pressure on departments that profile or use excessive force. Communities also gain grant-funded civilian review boards and independent investigations of officer-involved deaths.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People subject to police stops and force

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the criminal intent standard for convicting an officer under the federal civil-rights statute from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly,' making federal prosecutions easier.
Limits qualified immunity so an officer cannot escape a civil lawsuit by claiming they did not know the conduct was unlawful or that the right was not clearly established.

Creates a public, searchable National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline, termination, and lawsuit records for federal and local officers, and conditions federal grant money on states having certification and decertification systems.
Bans no-knock warrants in drug cases, restricts chokeholds and carotid holds, and establishes a national use-of-force standard for federal officers (the PEACE Act).

Requires federal, state, and local agencies to report stops, searches, and use of force disaggregated by race, ethnicity, and gender, with federal grant money withheld from states that fail to report.
Authorizes roughly $1 billion in grants for independent investigations of officer-involved deaths, state pattern-or-practice investigations, civilian review boards, and body cameras.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new grant programs and registry (over $1 billion authorized for fiscal years 2026-2028). Police departments and their insurers bear higher litigation exposure from the narrowed defenses, and local governments face costs for data systems, accreditation, body cameras, and revised use-of-force policies. States that refuse the new reporting and certification rules lose federal Byrne and COPS grant funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes more than $1 billion in new federal spending for fiscal years 2026-2028, adding to the deficit unless offset.

Police organizations and many state and local governments argue that removing qualified immunity and lowering the intent standard would expose individual officers and their municipalities to more lawsuits and drive up liability costs; the bill also strips a department's federal grants if a union contract blocks the Attorney General from enforcing a consent decree, which union opponents call federal overreach into collective bargaining.

Grant conditioning cuts both ways: states that decline the bill's reporting, accreditation, and training requirements would forfeit federal police grant money, reducing funds available for local public safety in noncomplying states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability changes go to the heart of a documented problem: qualified immunity and the 'willfulness' standard have made it extremely difficult to sue or convict officers who injure or kill civilians. The main honest costs are fiscal (over $1 billion in authorized grants) and the risk that higher liability and stricter decertification make police recruitment harder. The grant-withholding mechanism is coercive but targeted. On balance, the bill's benefits for people who encounter police are large relative to its costs, and its design is more detailed than typical oversight legislation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced; none has taken it up, no hearing or markup has been held, and no floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Ivey introduced H.R. 5361 in the House on September 15, 2025, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, the Armed Services and Energy and Commerce Committees.
It has 136 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican has signed on.
The full action history shows only introduction and committee referral, with no subsequent action by any committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change: police departments, unions, and accreditation bodies remain unbound because no committee has acted, while the bill's 137 Democratic supporters have nothing to show for their support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Departments and unions, so far untouched

for.name: Rep. Glenn Ivey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act of 2025 in the House and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 136 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosigned the bill, giving it the largest cosponsor list of any House police-reform bill this Congress but no Republican support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill since its September 2025 referral.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; with a Republican majority and no Republican cosponsors, no vote is scheduled.

against.name: Police unions, including the Fraternal Order of Police
against.what_they_did: Opposed comparable police-accountability legislation in prior Congresses, particularly qualified-immunity changes and restrictions on collective bargaining provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic: all 136 cosponsors are Democrats and none is a Republican, and the Republican-controlled House has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Police unions and law enforcement labor organizations
industries.note: The bill removes qualified immunity as a defense, narrows the criminal intent standard, creates a public misconduct registry, and cuts federal grants to departments whose union contracts block federal consent-decree enforcement. Its interest in shielding officers from civil liability and discipline runs directly against the bill's accountability goals.

The bill directs the Justice Department to develop uniform accreditation standards and requires grant recipients to spend at least 5% of awards on gaining accreditation from these private organizations, making them a permanent gatekeeper over federal police grant money.

industries.industry: Body camera and police technology vendors
industries.note: The bill mandates body cameras for federal officers and recording equipment in patrol vehicles, funded through grants, creating a large mandated market for this equipment while serving the public's interest in recorded encounters.

The bill restricts federal law enforcement's use of facial recognition technology on body camera and vehicle footage, cutting off a growing market, a restriction that privacy advocates view as protecting the public.

The bill includes the Stop Militarizing Law Enforcement Act, which curbs federal programs that supply military-grade equipment to local police departments, reducing a revenue channel for weapons and tactical gear makers.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority and not one Republican cosponsor, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote this Congress and will probably sit in committee until it expires — the same fate as most Democratic police-reform bills in recent Congresses. A nearly identical version did pass a Democratic-controlled House in 2021 but died in the Senate, so even a floor win would not be decisive.
